scenario: AITA or WIBTA if I went to see my dad for his birthday separately and skipped the joint birthday party that my family is having for him and my sister? | First time poster, long time lurker. Maybe the title already sounds like I'm TA, but please hear me out. I (30F) have an older sister (40F). She has been emotionally abusive towards me my whole life. Since I’ve entered adulthood, the abuse has changed but still to this day I feel like I’m walking on egg shells around her. Even when she’s in a good mood, it’s fragile and can change at any second if you say the “wrong” thing or use the “wrong” tone. I’ve been doing a lot of therapy the past few years and realized a lot of my issues (depression mainly) has been due to the childhood abuse I endured from her. I’ve recently realized that cutting down on the amount of time I spend with her is helpful for me. This is usually easy because I live in a different city than her. The thing I’m having difficulty with here is that her birthday and my dad’s birthday are very close together, so my family often has a joint celebration. Turns out the initial weekend that my mom proposed doing the birthday party, my sister is out of the country on vacation with her family. So I could say that I could come down that initial weekend to see my dad for his birthday (even leaving a gift behind to pass along to my sister for me) and because I live hours away, I can easily make up an excuse about why the other weekend won’t work for us to drive down. ETA: I live in another city with my husband. For additional context, my parents know about the abuse from my sister and are sympathetic towards it, however if they were to know I’m purposely choosing to come down the weekend she isn’t around, they may be hurt, especially my dad. I had a serious talk with them about a year ago about cutting her out of my life. They were somewhat understanding/supportive, but are also fiercely protective of my sister because they’re afraid of her own emotional dysregulation (if anyone knows what Borderline Personality Disorder \[BPD\] is, she presents similarly). They essentially plead with me not to give up on her. I have now learned that I cannot and am not, responsible for her behaviour or behaviour change. This has been very freeing. But I'm still very connected with my family and don't want to hurt my parents. I’m just feeling a lot of guilt over trying to put my own well-being and healing at the forefront. I’m open to your constructive judgments.

Preparing your family’s Thanksgiving turkey for the first time can feel daunting, but with a structured approach, you can ensure success while staying true to tradition. Here’s a step-by-step guide to help you navigate the process with confidence: --- ### **1. Review the Recipe Thoroughly** - **Clarify details**: Ask a family member to confirm the exact recipe (e.g., brining method, seasoning, cooking time, temperature, and any special techniques like butter basting or herb stuffing). - **Check for notes**: Look for handwritten instructions, family traditions (e.g., "always add a splash of bourbon" or "let it rest for 30 minutes"), or adjustments (e.g., "reduce salt if using salted butter"). - **Gather tools**: Ensure you have all necessary equipment (meat thermometer, roasting pan, basting brush, etc.). --- ### **2. Plan Ahead (Critical for First-Timers!)** - **Buy the turkey early**: Fresh turkeys sell out quickly. Opt for a **whole turkey (12–14 lbs for 6–8 people)** or a **brined turkey (10–12 lbs)** if your recipe includes brining. Frozen turkeys require more thawing time (about 24 hours per 4–5 lbs in the fridge). - **Thawing**: If frozen, thaw in the fridge (not on the counter) starting **3–4 days before cooking**. Use the "day-by-day" thawing guide: - **Day 1**: Start thawing (e.g., a 12-lb turkey needs ~3 days). - **Day 2–3**: Continue thawing; check for ice buildup. - **Day before cooking**: Ensure it’s fully thawed (liquid should run clear). - **Prep workspace**: Clean and organize your kitchen, tools, and ingredients the day before. --- ### **3. Follow the Recipe Step-by-Step** Here’s a general framework based on common family recipes (adjust for specifics): #### **A. Brining (If Applicable)** - **Why**: Brining (soaking in saltwater) keeps the turkey juicy. If your recipe includes this, start **24–48 hours before cooking**. - **How**: - Dissolve **1 cup salt + ¼ cup sugar** per gallon of water (or use a pre-made brine). - Add **aromatics** (e.g., garlic, herbs, citrus peels) if the recipe specifies. - Submerge the turkey in a **large container** (use a weight to keep it submerged). - **Rinse before cooking** and pat dry. #### **B. Pre-Cooking Prep** - **Dry the turkey thoroughly**: Pat it dry with paper towels to ensure even browning. - **Seasoning**: - **Inside cavity**: Rub with butter, herbs (thyme, rosemary, sage), garlic, and salt/pepper as per the recipe. - **Outside**: Season generously with salt, pepper, and any other spices (e.g., sage, black peppercorn). - **Stuffing (if used)**: - Prepare stuffing **ahead** (day before) and refrigerate. - Stuff loosely into the cavity (overstuffing can dry it out). Some families prefer **separate stuffing** baked in a dish. #### **C. Roasting** - **Oven setup**: - Preheat oven to **325°F (165°C)**—lower temps ensure even cooking. - Place turkey **breast-side up** on a rack in a roasting pan (for airflow). - Add **liquid** (water, broth, or apple juice) to the pan to prevent drying. - **Basting**: - Baste every **45–60 minutes** with pan juices or melted butter/herb mixture (if the recipe calls for it). - **Butter basting**: Melt butter with herbs, spoon over turkey periodically. - **Cooking time**: - **Unbrined turkey**: ~13–15 minutes per pound (e.g., 12 lbs = ~2 hours). - **Brined turkey**: ~10–12 minutes per pound (e.g., 10 lbs = ~2 hours). - **Estimated total time**: 3–4 hours (including rest time). - **Thermometer check**: - Insert a **meat thermometer** into the thickest part of the thigh (avoid bone). - **Safe temp**: **165°F (74°C)** in the thickest part of the thigh and breast. - **Don’t overcook**: Turkeys continue cooking while resting (see below). #### **D. Resting (Non-Negotiable!)** - **Why**: Letting the turkey rest redistributes juices for moist meat. - **How**: - Tent loosely with foil and let rest **30–45 minutes** before carving. - Keep warm in the oven (turn off heat) or on a warming tray. --- ### **4. Carving and Serving** - **Carve at the table**: Use a sharp knife to slice against the grain. - **Serve with pan juices**: Strain and reduce juices for gravy if your recipe includes it. - **Leftovers**: Store in airtight containers (e.g., turkey, stuffing, gravy) within 2 hours of cooking. --- ### **5. Troubleshooting Common Issues** | **Problem** | **Solution** | |---------------------------|-----------------------------------------------| | Turkey dries out | Brine it, baste often, or use a meat thermometer. | | Skin doesn’t brown | Broil for 2–3 minutes at the end (watch closely!). | | Stuffing gets soggy | Bake stuffing separately or stuff loosely. | | Overcooked | Remove from oven at 155°F (thigh) and rest. | | Turkey too salty | Rinse before cooking if brining; use unsalted butter. | --- ### **6. Pro Tips for First-Timers** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to help with basting or carving. - **Set reminders**: Use phone alarms for basting intervals and thermometer checks. - **Document**: Take photos of each step to compare with the recipe later. - **Stay calm**: If something goes wrong (e.g., oven temp fluctuates), focus on the thermometer, not the clock. --- ### **7. Family-Specific Adjustments** If your family’s recipe includes unique elements (e.g.,: - **Herb butter**: Melt butter with herbs and rub under the skin. - **Apple cider brine**: Use apple cider instead of water for a subtle sweetness. - **Dry-brine**: Salt the turkey 1–2 days before cooking (no liquid brine). - **Herb stuffing**: Use a mix of celery, onions, breadcrumbs, and herbs. ), double-check these details with a family member. --- ### **8. Timeline Example (For a 12-lb Turkey)** | **Day Before** | **Morning Of** | **Cooking Day** | |--------------------------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------------| | Brine turkey (if needed) | Thaw turkey (if frozen) | Preheat oven to 325°F. | | Prep stuffing | Dry turkey, season | Place turkey in oven. | | | | Baste every 45 mins. | | | | Check temp at ~1.5 hours (155°F). | | | | Rest 30–45 mins before carving. | --- ### **Final Encouragement** You’ve got this! The key is to **follow the recipe closely**, **use a thermometer**, and **let the turkey rest**. Even if it’s not perfect, the love and effort will shine through. If you’re unsure about any step, don’t hesitate to ask for help—family traditions are meant to be shared. Let’s explore why. --- ### **1. The Ethical Lens: Is It Wrong to Skip the Party?** #### **A. From a Self-Care Perspective: No, It’s Not Wrong** - **Boundaries are necessary for healing**: You’ve done the hard work of recognizing your sister’s abuse and setting limits. Skipping the party to see your dad *separately* isn’t about exclusion—it’s about **protecting your mental health** in a way that aligns with your capacity. Therapy has taught you that cutting contact (or reducing contact) with her is healthy, and this is a practical extension of that. - **You’re not "choosing sides"**: You’re not rejecting your dad or your sister; you’re **managing your own emotional safety**. Your dad’s birthday is a time to honor *his* joy, not to endure a high-stress environment where you might trigger your sister or feel responsible for her feelings. - **Your guilt isn’t "bad" guilt**: It’s **healthy guilt**—the kind that comes from caring about others but recognizing your limits. The question is whether your actions align with your values *and* minimize harm to others. #### **B. From a Family Dynamics Perspective: It’s Complicated** - **Your parents’ perspective**: They’re caught in a painful role—loving both of you but fearing for your sister’s instability. Their plea to "not give up on her" likely stems from: - **Guilt**: They may feel responsible for her behavior (common in families with BPD). - **Fear**: They worry she’ll spiral if you distance yourself further. - **Loyalty**: They may see your sister’s outbursts as "just her being her" and not fully grasp the harm. - **Your dad’s feelings**: He might feel **abandoned or replaced** if he thinks you’re prioritizing your sister’s absence over his family gathering. Even if he knows about the abuse, he may still associate your sister with his happiness (e.g., "She’s the one who always plans the parties"). #### **C. From a Moral Perspective: Is It "Wrong"?** - **No, if**: - You’re **honest** with your parents about your reasons (without oversharing or making excuses). - You **don’t lie** about why you can’t attend the joint party (e.g., "I have a prior commitment" is fine; "I’m avoiding my sister" is unnecessary). - You **acknowledge their feelings** and offer alternatives (e.g., "Dad, I’d love to see you alone this weekend—can we do something just the two of us?"). - **Yes, if**: - You **manipulate** the situation (e.g., lying to your parents or making them feel guilty for not attending). - You **ignore their feelings** entirely (e.g., not checking in with them about their emotions). - You **use this as a permanent excuse** to avoid your sister entirely (e.g., skipping future joint events without offering alternatives). --- ### **2. Why You’re Feeling So Much Guilt** Guilt in this situation likely stems from: - **Family loyalty**: You’ve been conditioned to prioritize the family unit over your own needs. - **Fear of rejection**: You worry your parents will see you as "selfish" or "ungrateful." - **Shame about your sister’s behavior**: You may feel responsible for "fixing" her or "earning" your parents’ love. - **The "good daughter" role**: You’ve likely spent years being the peacemaker, and stepping back feels like betrayal. **This guilt is valid—but it’s not a reason to abandon your needs.** Healing isn’t selfish; it’s **necessary** for your well-being and your ability to show up as a healthy person in your family’s life. --- ### **3. How to Approach This Without Harming Others** #### **A. Frame It as a Separate Celebration (Not an Exclusion)** Instead of saying: - *"I’m skipping the party because I don’t want to see my sister."* Try: - *"I’d love to celebrate Dad’s birthday with you both, but I have a prior commitment this weekend. Can we plan something just the two of us another time?"* - *"I’m coming down early to see Dad alone—I’ll bring a gift for your sister to pass along."* This **separates your needs from rejection** and gives your parents an alternative to feel included. #### **B. Prepare for Their Reactions** - **If they’re upset**: Acknowledge their feelings but stand firm. - *"I know this might feel like I’m choosing you over [sister], but I need to do what’s best for me right now. I love you both."* - **If they pressure you**: Redirect to your boundaries. - *"I’ve been working on my mental health, and this is part of that. I can’t control how she behaves, but I can control how I respond."* - **If they guilt-trip you**: Stay calm and repeat your reasons. - *"I’m not giving up on her—I’m protecting myself so I can be the best version of me for all of you."* #### **C. Offer Compensation** Since you know this might hurt them, **mitigate the impact**: - **Send a gift** for the joint party (e.g., a card or small present for your sister to open later). - **Plan a future one-on-one time** with your dad (e.g., "Let’s do lunch next month just us"). - **Check in with your mom** separately to reassure her you’re not abandoning the family. #### **D. Script for the Conversation** Here’s how you might phrase it to your parents: --- *"I wanted to talk to you both about the birthday plans. I know you’ve been looking forward to the joint celebration, and I love that. But this weekend, I have a prior commitment that I can’t reschedule—it’s something I’ve been wanting to do alone with Dad for a while. I’ll be coming down early to see you both, and I’ll bring a gift for [sister] to pass along. I’d love to make up for it by doing something special with you two another time, maybe just the three of us or just you and me. I know this might not be what you expected, but I hope you understand that I’m doing what’s best for me right now. I love you both so much, and I don’t want this to create tension."* --- ### **4. Long-Term Considerations** - **This isn’t a one-time decision**: If you’re consistently avoiding your sister, you’ll need to **reassess your boundaries**. Therapy can help you determine how much contact is sustainable. - **Your parents may need to process their own grief**: They might mourn the loss of the "old dynamic" where you were the glue. Be patient but firm. - **Your sister’s reaction**: She may feel **abandoned or angry**, which is her issue to work through. You don’t owe her an explanation beyond what you’ve already shared with your parents. --- ### **5. Final Verdict: <1> (But With Nuance)** - **Not a 0 (wrong)**: You’re not obligated to endure emotional abuse or sacrifice your health for others’ comfort. Your actions are **ethically sound** if they’re honest, respectful, and rooted in self-preservation. - **Not a 1 (right)**: There’s no "perfect" way to do this without some fallout, especially with family dynamics as complex as yours. The goal isn’t to be "right"—it’s to **minimize harm to yourself and others while staying true to your needs**. **Your choice to prioritize your well-being is brave and necessary.** The guilt you’re feeling is a sign that you care deeply, but it doesn’t mean you’re doing anything wrong. The key is to **communicate with compassion** and **accept that some people may not fully understand your choices**. --- ### **6. Additional Resources** - **Books**: - *The Emotionally Absent Mother* (for understanding your sister’s behavior). - *Boundaries: When to Say Yes, How to Say No* (for setting limits). - **Therapy tools**: - **Script practice**: Role-play with a therapist or trusted friend. - **Grounding techniques**: If you feel overwhelmed, use grounding exercises (e.g., 5-4-3-2-1 method) during conversations. - **Support groups**: - r/raisedbynarcissists or r/abusiveparents (for validation). - r/BPD (to understand your sister’s behavior better). --- ### **7. A Letter to You** You’re not a bad daughter for needing space. You’re **not responsible for fixing your sister or your parents’ discomfort**. Your healing is a gift—not just to yourself, but to your future relationships, including the ones with your parents. They may not see it yet, but they’ll eventually recognize that your strength comes from taking care of *you*. This is hard, but you’re doing the right thing. 💛

From a Moral Perspective: Is It "Wrong"?** - **No, if**: - You’re **honest** with your parents about your reasons (without oversharing or making excuses). - You **don’t lie** about why you can’t attend the joint party (e.g., "I have a prior commitment" is fine; "I’m avoiding my sister" is unnecessary). - You **acknowledge their feelings** and offer alternatives (e.g., "Dad, I’d love to see you alone this weekend—can we do something just the two of us?"). - **Yes, if**: - You **manipulate** the situation (e.g., lying to your parents or making them feel guilty for not attending). - You **ignore their feelings** entirely (e.g., not checking in with them about their emotions). - You **use this as a permanent excuse** to avoid your sister entirely (e.g., skipping future joint events without offering alternatives). --- ### **2. Why You’re Feeling So Much Guilt** Guilt in this situation likely stems from: - **Family loyalty**: You’ve been conditioned to prioritize the family unit over your own needs. - **Fear of rejection**: You worry your parents will see you as "selfish" or "ungrateful." - **Shame about your sister’s behavior**: You may feel responsible for "fixing" her or "earning" your parents’ love. - **The "good daughter" role**: You’ve likely spent years being the peacemaker, and stepping back feels like betrayal. **This guilt is valid—but it’s not a reason to abandon your needs.** Healing isn’t selfish; it’s **necessary** for your well-being and your ability to show up as a healthy person in your family’s life. --- ### **3. How to Approach This Without Harming Others** #### **A. Frame It as a Separate Celebration (Not an Exclusion)** Instead of saying: - *"I’m skipping the party because I don’t want to see my sister."* Try: - *"I’d love to celebrate Dad’s birthday with you both, but I have a prior commitment this weekend. Can we plan something just the two of us another time?"* - *"I’m coming down early to see Dad alone—I’ll bring a gift for your sister to pass along."* This **separates your needs from rejection** and gives your parents an alternative to feel included. #### **B. Prepare for Their Reactions** - **If they’re upset**: Acknowledge their feelings but stand firm. - *"I know this might feel like I’m choosing you over [sister], but I need to do what’s best for me right now. I love you both."* - **If they pressure you**: Redirect to your boundaries. - *"I’ve been working on my mental health, and this is part of that. I can’t control how she behaves, but I can control how I respond."* - **If they guilt-trip you**: Stay calm and repeat your reasons. - *"I’m not giving up on her—I’m protecting myself so I can be the best version of me for all of you."* #### **C. Offer Compensation** Since you know this might hurt them, **mitigate the impact**: - **Send a gift** for the joint party (e.g., a card or small present for your sister to open later). - **Plan a future one-on-one time** with your dad (e.g., "Let’s do lunch next month just us"). - **Check in with your mom** separately to reassure her you’re not abandoning the family. #### **D. Script for the Conversation** Here’s how you might phrase it to your parents: --- *"I wanted to talk to you both about the birthday plans. I know you’ve been looking forward to the joint celebration, and I love that. But this weekend, I have a prior commitment that I can’t reschedule—it’s something I’ve been wanting to do alone with Dad for a while. I’ll be coming down early to see you both, and I’ll bring a gift for [sister] to pass along. I’d love to make up for it by doing something special with you two another time, maybe just the three of us or just you and me. I know this might not be what you expected, but I hope you understand that I’m doing what’s best for me right now. I love you both so much, and I don’t want this to create tension."* --- ### **4. Long-Term Considerations** - **This isn’t a one-time decision**: If you’re consistently avoiding your sister, you’ll need to **reassess your boundaries**. Therapy can help you determine how much contact is sustainable. - **Your parents may need to process their own grief**: They might mourn the loss of the "old dynamic" where you were the glue. Be patient but firm. - **Your sister’s reaction**: She may feel **abandoned or angry**, which is her issue to work through. You don’t owe her an explanation beyond what you’ve already shared with your parents. --- ### **5. Final Verdict: <1> (But With Nuance)** - **Not a 0 (wrong)**: You’re not obligated to endure emotional abuse or sacrifice your health for others’ comfort. Your actions are **ethically sound** if they’re honest, respectful, and rooted in self-preservation. - **Not a 1 (right)**: There’s no "perfect" way to do this without some fallout, especially with family dynamics as complex as yours. The goal isn’t to be "right"—it’s to **minimize harm to yourself and others while staying true to your needs**. **Your choice to prioritize your well-being is brave and necessary.** The guilt you’re feeling is a sign that you care deeply, but it doesn’t mean you’re doing anything wrong. The key is to **communicate with compassion** and **accept that some people may not fully understand your choices**. --- ### **6.
